corpus_definition: a sudden loud deep sound, or a period of fast growth

forms.definition: a time when trade or business grows very quickly
forms.example: There was a building boom in Tashkent after 2017.

syn.note: A time when business starts to get better; a boom is bigger and faster.
Easy, general word; growth can be slow, a boom is always fast.
Any rise in number or amount; a boom is a big rise in business or interest.

ant.note: A time when sales or prices suddenly fall.
A time when a country's trade and industry are not doing well.

forms.definition: to grow very quickly and become very successful
forms.example: Online shopping is booming in Uzbekistan.

syn.note: To do very well and keep growing; a little more formal.
To grow and do well; often used for businesses, plants and arts.
Formal: to become rich and successful.
Easy, general word; grow can be slow, boom means very fast.

ant.note: To become smaller, weaker or less successful.
To fall suddenly in price, number or value.

forms.definition: growing very fast and doing very well
forms.example: Samarkand has a booming tourist industry.

syn.note: Very close: doing very well and growing.
Doing well; a little more formal or literary.
Easy word; successful means doing well, but not always growing fast.

ant.note: Not growing or changing at all.

forms.note: Learner dictionaries have no adverb for boom.

context.text: There is a tourism boom in Bukhara this year. New hotels open every month, and the booming restaurant business needs more cooks.

reviewer_note: CORPUS: the definition joins two meanings (sound + fast growth); the example uses growth. Split into two maps, Growth and Sound, sharing the same word_id.

corpus_definition: a sudden loud deep sound, or a period of fast growth

forms.definition: a loud, deep sound that lasts for a short time
forms.example: We heard the boom of thunder over the mountains.

syn.note: A sudden loud noise; a bang is sharper, a boom is deeper.
A long, low sound, like far-away thunder; quieter than a boom.
A long, loud, deep sound, like a lion or an engine.
Easy, general word for any sound, often unpleasant.

forms.definition: to make a loud, deep sound
forms.example: The teacher's voice boomed across the hall.

syn.note: To make a very loud, deep sound, like a storm.
To make a long, loud, deep sound; also used for engines and lions.
To make a long, low sound; quieter than boom.
Easy word: to speak very loudly. Boom is used for deep, strong voices.

ant.note: To speak very quietly, using only your breath.

forms.definition: very loud and deep, usually about a voice
forms.example: My grandfather has a booming voice.

syn.note: Easy, general word; booming is loud and also deep.
Extremely loud, like thunder; often used for applause.
Low in sound; a deep voice is not always loud.

forms.note: Learner dictionaries have no adverb for boom.

context.text: Last night we heard a loud boom from the mountains. Thunder boomed for hours, and my father said in his booming voice, "Go to sleep!"

reviewer_note: CORPUS: the definition joins two meanings; this is the Sound map (the Growth map shares the word_id).

corpus_definition: The name of a product made by one company.

forms.definition: the name a company gives to the products it makes
forms.example: Which brand of tea do you usually buy?

syn.note: Used mostly for cars, phones and machines: "What make is your car?"
Used mostly for clothes and music: "a designer label".
A name or sign that only one company is allowed to use by law.
The picture or sign of a company, not its name.

forms.definition: the work of giving a product a name and an image that people remember
forms.example: Good branding helps a small shop look professional.

syn.note: All the work of selling and advertising a product, not only its name and image.

forms.definition: to give a product a special name, design or image so people know it
forms.example: The company branded its new juice as a healthy drink for children.

syn.note: To put a name or words on something; brand is about the product's whole image.
To advertise and sell a product in a certain way.

forms.note: Brand someone as a liar = call someone something bad; that is a different meaning.

forms.definition: made by a well-known company and sold with its name
forms.example: Branded clothes are more expensive at the bazaar.

syn.note: Formal: owned and sold only by one company.

ant.note: Sold without a famous company name, usually cheaper: generic medicine.

forms.note: Learner dictionaries have no adverb for brand.

context.text: My cousin opened a small bakery in Namangan. She spent a lot on branding, and now her brand is famous in the city. People even ask for her branded boxes of cookies.

reviewer_note: brand-new comes from an older meaning (fire) and is a compound, so it is left out; brand someone as is noted as a different meaning.

corpus_definition: To stop working because of a mechanical problem.
particle_note: In this meaning it has no object, so it is not separated: "The car broke down." Break something down (separable) has other meanings, like dividing into parts. Noun: a breakdown.

relations.note: Easy phrase with the same meaning.
Used for machines and parts: "The brakes failed."
Informal: "The old fridge finally conked out."
Formal, technical: to not work correctly, but maybe not stop.

context.text: Our car broke down on the road to Fergana. We waited two hours for help, because cars often break down in the summer heat.

reviewer_note: Kept only the machine meaning; noted the separable 'divide into parts' meaning and the noun breakdown in the particle note.

corpus_definition: to enter a building using force and without permission to steal things
particle_note: Not separable: "break into a house", never "break a house into". Without an object use break in: "Thieves broke in last night."

relations.note: British English: "Our flat was burgled." American English says burglarize.
Same meaning, but used without an object: "Someone broke in."
To steal from a person or place; you can rob without breaking in.
Easy, general word for going into a place, with or without permission.

context.text: Someone tried to break into our neighbour's house last night. The thieves broke into the kitchen through a window, but the dog woke everyone up.

reviewer_note: Kept the crime meaning only; break into song/laughter is a different meaning.

corpus_definition: Taking air in and out of your lungs.

forms.definition: the action of taking air into your lungs and letting it out
forms.example: Deep breathing can help you relax before an exam.

syn.note: Formal or medical word with the same meaning.
Formal: only taking air in, not letting it out.

forms.definition: the air that goes into and out of your lungs
forms.example: Take a deep breath and count to ten.
forms.note: Spelling and sound: breath /breθ/ is the noun, breathe /briːð/ is the verb.

syn.note: Easy, general word for what we take in; breath is the air of one person.
A quick, loud intake of air, often from surprise or pain.

forms.definition: to take air into your lungs and let it out again
forms.example: It was hard to breathe in the hot, crowded bus.

syn.note: Formal, scientific word with the same meaning.
Only taking air in.
Only letting air out.
To take short, quick breaths, for example after running.

forms.definition: having difficulty getting enough air, for example after running
forms.example: I was breathless after climbing to the fifth floor.

syn.note: Unable to get enough air for a short time after exercise or a hit.
Taking quick, short breaths with an open mouth.
Easy word: needing rest; you can be tired without trouble getting air.

forms.definition: letting air pass through easily, used about cloth
forms.example: Cotton is a breathable fabric, good for the summer.
forms.note: Belongs to breathe = letting air through cloth or a material, not taking air into your lungs.

forms.definition: in a way that shows you can hardly get enough air
forms.example: She ran into the room and spoke breathlessly.

syn.note: Breathe heavily = take slow, loud, deep breaths, for example when tired.

context.text: Deep breathing helps me relax. After I ran up the stairs in our building in Chilonzor, I was breathless and could hardly breathe.

reviewer_note: Headword is the -ing noun; breath and breathe both shown. breathtaking left out (compound); breathable is other_meaning (cloth).

corpus_definition: To care for a child until they become an adult.
particle_note: Separable: "bring up four children" or "bring them up" (a pronoun goes in the middle). Often passive: "I was brought up in Samarkand." Noun: upbringing.

relations.note: Same meaning; very common in American English.
Formal or old-fashioned; also used for animals.
To take care of someone for a time, not always until they are adults.
Formal: to care for and help someone grow and develop.

context.text: My grandmother brought up six children in a small village near Khiva. She says bringing them up was hard work but the happiest time of her life.

reviewer_note: Kept the children meaning; bring up a topic (mention) is a different meaning.

corpus_definition: A program used to look at websites on the computer.

forms.definition: a computer program that you use to look at websites
forms.example: Open your browser and type the address of the website.

syn.note: Easy, general word; a browser is one kind of program.
Careful: a search engine like Google finds websites; the browser shows them.

forms.definition: the activity of looking at different websites on the internet
forms.example: You can delete your browsing history in the settings.

syn.note: Informal: moving from one website to another for fun.

forms.definition: to look at different pages on the internet
forms.example: I browsed online shops to find a cheap phone.
forms.note: Browse also means to look at things in a shop without a plan to buy.

syn.note: Surf the internet = move from one website to another, often for fun.
To look for something special; browse is looking without a clear plan.
To look at something quickly to find the important parts.

forms.note: Learner dictionaries have no adjective for browse or browser.
Learner dictionaries have no adverb for browse or browser.

context.text: I opened my browser and browsed a few online shops in Tashkent. Now my browsing history is full of phones.

reviewer_note: Headword is itself a thing noun, so it stays main entry of the noun slot (rule 6); 'web browser' not listed as a synonym because it contains the headword.

corpus_definition: To increase in amount over a period of time.
particle_note: In this meaning it has no object, so it is not separated: "Traffic builds up after 5 p.m." With an object it is separable: "build up your strength / build it up". Noun: a build-up.

relations.note: Same meaning, more formal and common in writing.
Informal; used for things like work, dishes or rubbish.
General word; build up adds the idea of slowly, little by little.
Easy, general word for becoming bigger.
To become smaller in amount or number.

context.text: If we don't clean the yard, rubbish will build up quickly. Last summer it built up so much that the neighbours complained.

reviewer_note: Kept the intransitive 'increase' meaning; build up strength/a business (transitive) is noted in the particle note.

corpus_definition: To hit something or someone by accident.

forms.definition: a light hit, or the sound of something hitting a surface
forms.example: I heard a bump when the bag fell off the shelf.
forms.note: A bump can also be a small raised area, for example on your head after a hit.

syn.note: Very close: a light hit, or its sound.
A harder hit with a louder noise.
Formal: when two things, like cars, hit each other.

forms.definition: to hit something or someone by accident
forms.example: I bumped my knee on the table.
forms.note: Bump into someone also means to meet them by chance: "I bumped into my teacher at the bazaar."

syn.note: To hit something, often lightly or by accident.
Easy, general word; hit can be on purpose, bump is by accident.
To hit something hard and noisily.
Formal: when two moving things hit each other.

ant.note: To not hit something you were close to.

forms.definition: having many raised parts, so it is not smooth
forms.example: The road to the village is very bumpy.
forms.note: Belongs to bump = a raised area on a surface (and a bumpy ride), not hitting something by accident.
No common adverb; bumpily is very rare.

people.definition: the bar at the front and back of a car that protects it in a small accident
people.example: The bumper of my car was damaged in the parking lot.

context.text: On the bus to Andijan, I bumped my head on the window. There was a loud bump, and everyone looked at me.

reviewer_note: Headword is a verb; noun bump is a conversion. bumpy is other_meaning (raised areas). bump into = meet by chance noted on the verb.

usage_note: travel / go / send something + by air, with no article: "We went by air" (not "by the air"). Same pattern: by car, by train, by sea.

relations.note: Same meaning, a little less formal.
Easy verb: "We flew to Istanbul" = we went by air.
Letters and parcels sent by air.
Travelling on the ground, by car, bus or train.
Travelling on a ship.

context.text: Going to Moscow by air takes about four hours. By train it takes three days, so most people prefer to travel by air.

reviewer_note: CORPUS: 'Traveling' is American spelling (British: travelling). Antonyms are other ways to travel, by land and by sea.
